Agent Matrix2026Personal project · Multi-agent workflow

Fourteen agents were waiting on me, so I designed how they ask.

I direct 14 AI agents building a game. They produce faster than I can review. This case is about designing how agents ask me, how I answer, and how the answer gets back to them, and about where the system still needed me when I was not there, and how I closed each gap.

Problem
Once the work was split across agents, output jumped. The morning after I set up a “waiting on you” table, it had 33 items opened and 22 still open. Questions put to me directly in a session were mostly answered within 20 minutes; the unprompted ones simply stayed open.
Key decisions
I kept the plan and the present as two separate layers; gave agents a fixed format for asking (the review card), where every card answers five questions and a decision can only come from me; and ran one batch per session, each ending with one page of state for a clean new session to pick up.
Outcome
I built a Feishu board, a review centre (live), session renewal, decision dispatch and a daily retrospective. The first time the dispatch delivered a real decision, the agent closed the card within two minutes.
Context
Personal project · the multi-agent workflow behind a game I am making
My role
Requirements, trade-off decisions and acceptance; documentation and development in collaboration with Claude
Timeline
Oct 2026 – ongoing
Deliverables
Feishu board, review centre (live), session renewal, decision dispatch, daily retrospective

01 · Starting point

One person, fourteen sessions.

I am making a 2D narrative management game adapted from Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland. I am the producer; 14 Claude agents each own one area: art direction, assets, gameplay code, script, publicity, plus a morning brief and a retrospective that run on a schedule. Each agent works in its own session and edits only its own folder. Only I can mark something as approved.

Once the work was split across agents, output jumped. I set up a “waiting on you” table to collect everything that needed me. By the next morning it had 33 items opened, 11 closed and 22 still open.

I noticed a pattern. Questions put to me directly in a session were mostly answered within 20 minutes. The unprompted “please look at this comparison” items simply stayed open.

Tobie’s note

The hard part is not getting agents to work. It is getting their questions to reach me in a form I can act on.

02 · Seeing

The plan and the present are two layers.

The first problem was visibility. With a dozen sessions running at once, I could not tell who was doing what, or who was stuck.

I did not put everything into one Gantt chart. The Gantt view shows the plan I set, in days and weeks. The board shows what each agent is doing right now, in minutes. The two are kept apart. I chose Feishu Base partly because its Gantt view supports dependencies natively.

Progress does not depend on agents remembering to report. Session hooks write status into the table automatically. When an agent does report, one command posts to the group chat, updates the table and logs the entry.

Tobie’s note

Checking the plan and checking the present are two different tasks. One view for both serves neither.

03 · The question format

Not another board. A format for asking.

With the board in place, I found that knowing something was waiting on me was not enough. What I said at the time: “I often don’t know what I’m supposed to be reviewing. Text alone doesn’t make it clear to me. It usually needs the images, or the story of how we got here.”

So what I needed was not another board. It was a fixed format for asking, plus a page where I could look at the images, annotate them and write my decision back. I call it a review card.

Every card has to answer five questions: what I am being asked to do, why we are at this point, where to look, what the options are, and what happens once I decide. A card missing any of them is rejected on submission. There are four kinds: accept, choose, do, and answer. An agent cannot approve its own work; a decision can only come from me, on the page.

The first version had 26 self-test items, and all 26 pass. Two of them failed in earlier rounds and passed only after fixes and a re-test.

One thing I did not expect. I had five example cards built from real screenshots, and I answered them as if they were real. When an example contains a real question, people treat it as real. Example cards now carry a label and stay out of the queue by default.

Tobie’s note

A good question turns “I need to think about this” into “I can decide at a glance.”

04 · Context

One batch, one session.

The second problem was usage. The longer a session runs, the more context is re-sent on every turn. I measured it once: 72% of the five-hour usage window was gone, and one session had been open for 15 hours.

The answer was one batch per session. When an agent hands over a batch, it writes the current state onto a single page and the session ends. A clean new session reads that page and picks up the next batch. A script checks that the page is complete before the handover counts.

Tobie’s note

Writing one page for the next session is more reliable than expecting one session to remember everything.

05 · The turn

Two fixes collided.

Review cards and one-batch sessions each solved their own problem. Together they created a new one I had not foreseen.

A session ends after its batch, and the successor only starts when I click to open it. When I did not click, the successors never started, and even work that did not need me stopped.

At the other end, I would give a decision on the page, but the session that had raised the card had already ended. Nobody was there to hear it.

I added two things. One command that lets me open every successor session in a single pass each day. And a scheduled task that, every half hour, delivers the decisions I have made to the agent concerned. The first time it delivered a real decision, the agent closed the card within two minutes.

Tobie’s note

Each fix was right on its own. What needs checking is whether a message can still travel the whole loop once they are combined.

06 · When I am not there

What stops, and how I closed each gap.

I cannot be online all the time. When I was slow to respond, the system showed four gaps. Each one is followed by what I did about it and where that stands.

1 · Done
Work that did not need me stopped too
One command to open all successor sessions; a scheduled task that delivers my decisions
2 · Done
I was away and could not open the cards
Moved the review centre to a server, usable from a phone
3 · Built, not deployed yet
I could open them, and they still waited
After 3 days, a non-urgent card proceeds on its recommended option, and I can reverse it later
4 · Not decided
Scheduled tasks depend on my laptop being awake
Move tasks like the morning brief to a cloud schedule

The key judgement sits between the second and third rows. I first assumed the problem was access, so I put the review centre online. The cards kept waiting. The retrospective’s reading was that the wait reflected whether I was online, not whether the cards were usable. The thing to fix was not the entrance. It was which decisions should never have been waiting for me.

The rule in the third row has limits too. Of the six cards that were waiting, it covers three: non-urgent choices that carry a recommended option. The two blocking acceptance cards and the one that needs me to act in person still wait for me. That is what the next section is about.

Tobie’s note

When I am away, the system should slow down, not stop.

07 · Reframing

I said switching mattered most. 203 cards said otherwise.

Once the review centre was live, I was getting 17 to 57 cards a day. The friction showed up one spot at a time: I wrote a line on a card, and an agent fixed it.

Nov 15 · Fixed
A card asked me to read a checklist but gave only a path on my computer. I couldn’t open it on my phone, and marked it done without reading it.
Files now travel with the card and open in the page, on a phone too.
Nov 17 · Fixed
Agents asked me again in chat about things I had already answered on the site.
Each card now records which session raised it, and a session checks for my answers before it asks me.
Nov 18 · Fixed
The progress page was just a list. I couldn’t tell how far things had got or what they looked like now.
Each project got a timeline, and every step opens to what it looks like now.

The biggest one was harder to fix. Each time I sat down, a median of 10 cards were waiting, and up to 42. I thought switching between cards was the problem, so I had an agent build a three-pane layout with the list beside the card. I rejected it with one line: don’t assume the problem is defined right; trace the second- and third-order effects.

It went back through 203 real cards. I handled a median of 2 per sitting, 55 seconds apart. 59% of the time I opened the newest card first; I never started with the oldest. 12% were sent back, and 33 needed a second version. Switching was not the slow part. There were too many cards, too fragmented, too hard to read. My own rejection notes said “I don’t know what exactly I’m meant to change” and “I can’t really see a difference.”

It came back with four options, each with its knock-on effects. Three panes would make the card a third narrower, and “I can’t see the difference” was already the most common reason for sending one back. I chose a one-line counter plus fixing the source. It then used the data to overrule two of my picks: acceptance cards with comparison images were sent back more often, not less; and I followed the recommended option only 73% of the time, too low to stop asking me.

What shipped were three small things: “N left · next” at the top of each card; earlier cards on the same thread listed under the header; non-urgent cards older than three days sink to the bottom. I pinned two problems on the first version’s screenshots, and the second version passed.

Tobie’s note

What I asked for was a solution, not necessarily my problem.

08 · Next

Fewer things that need me at all.

Everything above makes waiting for me smoother. The deeper fix is to have fewer things wait for me.

I have just started using trust levels, four of them, set per type of task. At the lowest level the AI states its plan at every step and acts only after I agree. It moves up a level after several consecutive results I did not need to change. Only at the top level can that type of task go into scheduled or batch runs. The approach follows a talk by Lauren Tan; the levels themselves were added by Claude.

Each time I correct something, the correction has to become a rule or a check, not one more sentence in a prompt.

Two things to watch next: whether the number of cards I have to decide each day falls as levels rise, and what still stops the next time I am away.

Tobie’s note

Trust is not handed over once. It is earned back, one type of task at a time.
